# 12 — Legs and wheels together: can one machine be efficient and gentle?

*Generated by [`analysis/hybrid_mobility.py`](../../analysis/hybrid_mobility.py); numbers in
[`hw/hybrid_mobility.json`](../../hw/hybrid_mobility.json). Round 16, answering the review's objection
to §11: tracks may be too damaging for the ground this robot works on.*

## The objection is right, but not for the reason it looks like

The first thing this study does is stop treating "gentle" as one property. It is three, and they
**point in opposite directions**:

| | What it damages | Best | Worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Contact pressure** | compacts soil, crushes roots | tracks, 5 kPa | **legs, 220 kPa** |
| **Disturbed area** | crushes vegetation | **legs, 0.034 m²/m** | tracks, 0.300 m²/m |
| **Shear** | tears turf and root mats | legs, none | skid steering, high |

![Ground impact](platform/hybrid-ground-impact.png)

Two things fall out immediately, and both are uncomfortable:

**1. Legs are not automatically gentle. As designed, this hexapod is the most damaging machine on the
page by contact pressure — 220 kPa, about 4 times a person's footfall and 47 times a track's.**
A third of a 190 kg robot lands on three 60 mm feet. That is a post-hole driver, not a light touch.
Fitting 140 mm compliant feet costs about 300 g a leg and drops it to 41 kPa — but it also raises
the disturbed area from 0.034 to 0.185 m² per metre, because a bigger foot touches more ground.
Foot area is a real design variable with a real trade behind it, and it has never been chosen deliberately.

**2. The damage the reviewer is worried about is caused by skid steering, not by the track.** A track's
contact pressure is the lowest of anything here (5 kPa). What tears the ground is the differential
slew, where both tracks scrub sideways through the turf. Replace skid steering with an articulated
centre pivot and the shear goes away for about 6 kg and one actuator, with pressure and disturbed
area unchanged. **That is the cheapest fix on this page and it was not in the round-15 recommendation.**

## What the hybrids actually cost

| Option | Machine (kg) | Energy (Wh/day) | Pressure (kPa) | Ground touched (m²/m) | Shear | Drive actuators |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hexapod, as designed | 190 | 4444 | 220 | 0.034 | none | 18 |
| Hexapod with 140 mm compliant feet | 192 | 4484 | 41 | 0.185 | none | 18 |
| Tracked, two tracks | 86 | 985 | 5 | 0.300 | high | 2 |
| Tracked, articulated steering | 92 | 1020 | 5 | 0.300 | low | 3 |
| Four steered wheels, no skid | 79 | 1039 | 15 | 0.240 | low | 8 |
| Wheel-on-leg (wheel is the foot) | 146 | 1470 | 27 | 0.240 | low | 16 |
| Wheel-on-leg with a deployable foot | 149 | 1483 | 32 | 0.103 | none | 16 |
| Tracked chassis carrying stowed legs | 195 | 1566 | 11 | 0.300 | high when rolling, none when walking | 14 |
| Tracked carrier + a 22 kg legged scout | 109 | 1224 | 9 | 0.095 | none | 14 |

![The trade](platform/hybrid-tradeoff.png)

**Carrying two locomotion systems is the worst answer.** A tracked chassis with stowed legs weighs
195 kg and burns 1566 Wh a day — heavier than the hexapod and 60 % more energy than plain
tracks — because it hauls both systems over every metre, and the legs have to be sized to lift the
tracks as well as the robot. This is the same mass fixed point that sank the hexapod, and it bites harder.

## The two answers worth building

**A. Articulated-steering tracks — 92 kg, 1020 Wh/day, 5 kPa, no shear.** If the sensitive ground is
mostly about compaction and turf damage rather than crushing individual plants, this is the whole answer.
It is one extra actuator on the round-15 recommendation and it removes the damage mechanism. It still
lays a 0.30 m² stripe per metre, so it is the wrong answer where the vegetation itself is what
must not be touched.

**B. A tracked carrier with a small legged scout — 109 kg, 1224 Wh/day, and on the sensitive ground
only a 22 kg machine at 9 kPa touching 0.095 m² per metre.** This is the option that actually
resolves the contradiction instead of compromising on it. The two requirements — cover distance
efficiently, and touch sensitive ground lightly — are in conflict only because we assumed one machine
has to do both. Split them and each gets what it needs: the carrier never enters the sensitive zone, and
the scout never has to carry a day's transit battery, which is why it can be 22 kg instead of 190.

It is the gentlest option on the page after the deployable-foot hybrid, at 1.2× the energy of plain
tracks and **a third of the energy of the wheel-on-leg hybrid**. It also fails gracefully: if the scout
is stuck or broken, the carrier still surveys, and vice versa.

**C. Wheel-on-leg with a deployable foot — 149 kg, 1483 Wh/day** — is the best single machine: it rolls
on wheels for transit and locks them to walk on a broad pad where the ground is sensitive. It is genuinely
the answer to the question as asked. But it costs 1.2× the marsupial's energy and 40 kg more, for
a harder controls problem and sixteen drive actuators, and it is still 50 % heavier than a tracked machine.

## What decides between them

Not something I can compute. It is **which damage mechanism actually matters on your ground**:

- If it is **compaction and rutting** — wet soil, root zones, archaeology — go with articulated tracks.
  They already have the lowest pressure of anything here and the pivot removes the shear.
- If it is **crushing the vegetation itself** — rare plants, seedling beds, cryptobiotic crust, moss —
  then disturbed area is the metric, and only a legged contact wins. Use the marsupial: keep the big
  machine out and send the scout in.
- If it is **both, everywhere, with no clean transit route**, the wheel-on-leg with a deployable foot is
  the single-machine answer, and you pay about 50 % more energy and mass than tracks for it.

## What is computed and what is assumed

Computed: every contact pressure and disturbed area, from foot and track geometry at each candidate's own
solved mass. Every energy figure, as a mass fixed point over the mixed route.

Assumed, and stated in the script: the route mix
(55% transit, 30% sensitive working ground, 10% difficult, 5% both);
the track and foot dimensions; the structure mass of everything except the legged base, which is this
project's measured robot; and the shear ranking, which is a judgement, not a measurement.

**The route mix is the number that decides this**, and it is a guess. A morning walking the actual site
with a tape and a camera would be worth more than another round of this analysis.

## Open items

1. **Which damage mechanism matters?** Compaction, crushing, or shear. This is a question for whoever
   owns the land, not for the model.
2. **Is there a clean transit route to each work site?** The marsupial depends on it.
3. **Foot area has never been chosen.** Even if the platform changes, 140 mm feet are a cheap improvement
   to whatever walks.
4. **Nothing here is a soil-mechanics model.** Pressure and disturbed area are proxies; real damage
   depends on moisture, soil type and repeat passes, none of which is modelled.
